slides.storyContext: A massive terracotta cube arrives at Priya's building. Arjun opens the manual: 'This cube holds exactly 3 cubic meters of soil. How many unit cubes fit inside?' Priya thinks: 'If each edge is 2 meters... 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cubes!'
slides.inSimpleWords: A cube number is multiplying a number three times.

image.alt: The Giant Cube Planter — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Perfect Cubes Defined

points.label: Definition
points.text: A perfect cube is a number multiplied by itself three times: n³ = n × n × n

points.label: Notation
points.text: The exponent 3 means 'multiply the base by itself twice.' Example: 4³ reads 'four cubed.'

points.label: 3D Context
points.text: 3³ = 27 means a 3×3×3 cube holds 27 unit cubes (like sugar cubes stacked in 3D)

slides.inSimpleWords: Perfect cubes are numbers that form 3D blocks.

slides.title: Stacking in 3D
slides.storyContext: Priya visualizes the planter: 2 meters deep, 2 meters wide, 2 meters tall. She layers: bottom layer is 2×2 = 4 unit cubes. Layer 2 is 4 more. Layer 3 is 4 more. Total: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12? No, wait. She recalculates: 2×2×2 = 8. Now it makes sense.
slides.inSimpleWords: Cubes stack in all three dimensions (length, width, height).

slides.title: Example 2: Terracotta Planter

example.problem: A cubic planter has edges of 4 meters. What volume of soil fits inside?
example.solution: Volume = length × width × height = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cubic meters. So 4³ = 64.

slides.inSimpleWords: 4 cubed equals 64 cubic meters volume.

image.alt: Example 2: Terracotta Planter — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Why Cubes Grow So Fast

points.label: Linear Growth
points.text: Double the side length: you double the distance (2x).

points.label: Square Growth
points.text: Double the side length: area becomes 2² = 4 times larger.

points.label: Cubic Growth
points.text: Double the side length: volume becomes 2³ = 8 times larger.

points.label: Example
points.text: 2³ = 8, but 3³ = 27 (more than 3 times larger), and 10³ = 1000 (100 times 10).

example.problem: If a 1-meter cube holds 1 cubic meter, how much does a 10-meter cube hold?
example.solution: 1³ = 1 cu.m. 10³ = 1000 cu.m. The 10-meter cube holds 1000 times more!

slides.inSimpleWords: Cubes grow much faster than their side length because volume involves three dimensions.

slides.title: Filling the Planter
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'So this cube with 3-meter edges holds 3³ = 27 cubic meters?' Priya nods. 'One bag of soil covers 1 cubic meter. We need 27 bags!' Arjun laughs: 'Good thing we know the math, or we'd order too few!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Cubing helps calculate volume for real building and gardening projects.

slides.title: Recognizing Perfect Cubes

points.label: Cube Roots
points.text: If 3³ = 27, then ∛27 = 3. The cube root reverses cubing.

points.label: Identifying Cubes
points.text: Is 8 a perfect cube? Yes, because 2³ = 8 (or ∛8 = 2).

points.label: Is 30 a Cube?
points.text: No. It sits between 3³ = 27 and 4³ = 64. No whole number cubed equals 30.

example.problem: Is 125 a perfect cube?

slides.inSimpleWords: Perfect cubes form a sequence; recognizing them helps with volume problems.

slides.title: Challenge 2: Cube Hunt

points.label: Question
points.text: Which of these are perfect cubes? 27, 64, 50, 125, 200, 216

example.problem: How do you identify perfect cubes?
example.solution: 27 = 3³. 64 = 4³. 125 = 5³. 216 = 6³. These are cubes. 50 and 200 are not.

slides.inSimpleWords: Recognizing cubes helps you estimate volumes quickly.

slides.title: Squares vs. Cubes: Comparison

points.label: Squares (n²)
points.text: Used for area (2D). Formula: side × side. Example: 5² = 25 sq. units.

points.label: Cubes (n³)
points.text: Used for volume (3D). Formula: side × side × side. Example: 5³ = 125 cu. units.

points.label: Growth
points.text: Cubes grow much faster than squares. 10² = 100, but 10³ = 1000.

points.label: Real Uses
points.text: Squares: land plots, painting walls. Cubes: shipping boxes, storage tanks, concrete blocks.

example.problem: A square plot is 5 m × 5 m. A cubic tank is 5 m × 5 m × 5 m. Compare areas vs. volumes.
example.solution: Plot area: 5² = 25 sq. m. Tank volume: 5³ = 125 cu. m. The cube is 5 times larger (125/25).

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares measure flat spaces; cubes measure 3D spaces and grow much faster.

slides.title: Planning Multiple Planters
slides.storyContext: Priya realizes one cube planter isn't enough for all her herbs. She wants 3 planters, each with 2-meter edges. Volume per planter: 2³ = 8 cu.m. Total: 3 × 8 = 24 cu.m. She orders 24 bags of soil. Arjun checks her math: perfect.
slides.inSimpleWords: Combining squares and cubes with multiplication solves complex projects.

slides.title: Example 3: Multiple Planters

example.problem: Priya wants 2 cubic planters, each with 2-meter edges. Total volume needed?
example.solution: One planter: 2³ = 8 cubic meters. Two planters: 2 × 8 = 16 cubic meters. Order 16 bags of soil.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine cubing with multiplication for real multi-object calculations.

slides.title: Scaling Problems with Squares and Cubes

points.label: Doubling Side Length
points.text: Area (square) becomes 2² = 4 times larger. Volume (cube) becomes 2³ = 8 times larger.

points.label: Tripling Side Length
points.text: Area becomes 3² = 9 times larger. Volume becomes 3³ = 27 times larger.

points.label: Cost Implication
points.text: If soil costs ₹100 per cubic meter, tripling planter size costs 27 times more.

points.label: Design Insight
points.text: Small changes in size create huge changes in material needs—plan carefully.

example.problem: Priya's original planter (2m) costs ₹800 to fill. If she triples the size (6m), how much will it cost?
example.solution: Original: 2³ = 8 cu.m. New: 6³ = 216 cu.m. Ratio: 216/8 = 27. Cost: ₹800 × 27 = ₹21,600.

slides.inSimpleWords: Scaling exponentially with squares and cubes affects material and cost.

slides.title: Real Example: Mumbai Building Code

example.problem: A builder in Mumbai plans cubic apartment blocks: 3 m × 3 m × 3 m per unit. How much air volume per unit?
example.solution: Volume = 3³ = 27 cubic meters. Building codes often require 35 cu. m per apartment for healthy living. This unit is too small; builder must expand.

slides.inSimpleWords: Knowing volumes helps ensure buildings meet safety and health standards.

slides.title: Challenge 3: Design Problem

points.label: Question
points.text: You have a square garden 7 m × 7 m. A cubic water tank has 2-meter edges. How much area for plants after the tank is placed?

example.problem: How do squares and cubes interact in real projects?
example.solution: Garden area: 7² = 49 sq. m. Tank footprint: 2² = 4 sq. m (base of cube). Plant area: 49 - 4 = 45 sq. m. Tank volume is separate (2³ = 8 cu. m).

slides.inSimpleWords: Real projects combine areas (squares) and volumes (cubes) in the same problem.

slides.title: Teaching the Next Generation
slides.storyContext: Priya's niece Ananya asks: 'How did you know how much soil to buy?' Priya sketches a 3×3 grid: 'This is 3². Count the squares: 9.' Then she stacks cubes: '3³ means three layers of 3×3. That's 27 cubes total.' Ananya's eyes light up. Priya realizes: 'Math is everywhere, and once you see it, you can solve any problem.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Understanding squares and cubes unlocks problem-solving power in any domain.

slides.title: The Garden Thrives
slides.storyContext: Months later, Priya's 8 × 8 meter garden (64 sq. m) blooms with herbs. The cubic planter (2³ = 8 cu. m) holds fresh soil. Arjun's calculations were perfect. They laugh about how numbers made their dream real. Math isn't abstract—it's in every meter they built.
slides.inSimpleWords: When you master squares and cubes, you can build anything you imagine.

slides.title: Squares and Cubes

points.text: Perfect squares (n²) are used for area of square plots and flat surfaces.
Perfect cubes (n³) are used for volume of cubic containers and 3D objects.
Priya designs gardens (areas), Arjun builds (volumes)—both use math daily in Mumbai.
Squares and cubes grow in predictable patterns: memorize the first 10 of each.
Real projects combine both: gardens with water tanks, buildings with rooms, storage with inventory.

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares and cubes help measure space and volume in every builder's and gardener's toolkit.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Bacteria Lab
hook: Arjun observes bacteria doubling every hour in his school science lab. 2, 4, 8, 16... By day 10, the count is huge. Priya uses exponents to predict it: 2¹⁰ = 1024. How does she do it so fast?

slides.title: Doubling Bacteria Count
slides.storyContext: Arjun's biology class grows bacteria in a petri dish. Day 1: 2 cells. Day 2: 4. Day 3: 8. By day 5, he counts 32 cells. 'But how do I predict day 10 without counting all week?' Priya smiles: 'Use powers. On day 10, you'll have 2 to the power 10.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents are shortcuts for repeated multiplication.

image.alt: Doubling Bacteria Count — Power Play

slides.title: What is an Exponent?

points.label: Simple Meaning
points.text: An exponent tells you how many times to multiply a number by itself.

points.label: Parts of aⁿ
points.text: a = base (the number being multiplied). n = exponent (how many times).

points.label: Shortcut Power
points.text: Instead of writing 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, we write 2⁵. Much faster!

slides.inSimpleWords: aⁿ means 'a times itself n times.'

slides.title: Arjun's Lab Discovery
slides.storyContext: Arjun carefully records the bacteria count each day. 'Look at the pattern!' says Priya, pointing at his notebook. 'Day 1 is 2¹, day 2 is 2², day 3 is 2³. By day 10, it's 2¹⁰ = 1024 bacteria!' Arjun's eyes widen. 'That's incredible. Without exponents, I'd need a huge table.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Patterns in nature often follow exponential growth.

slides.title: Exponent Notation

points.label: Definition
points.text: aⁿ means 'a multiplied by itself n times.' a is the base, n is the exponent or power.

points.label: Reading
points.text: 2³ = 'two to the power three' or 'two cubed' = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8

points.label: Zero Exponent
points.text: Any number to the power 0 equals 1: a⁰ = 1 (e.g., 5⁰ = 1)

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents show how many times to multiply.

image.alt: Exponent Notation — Power Play

slides.title: Example 1: Bacteria Growth

example.problem: On day 6, Arjun has 2⁶ bacteria. Calculate the count.
example.solution: 2⁶ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 64 bacteria on day 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: 2 to the power 6 is 64 bacteria.

image.alt: Example 1: Bacteria Growth — Power Play

slides.title: Challenge 1: Find the Exponent

example.problem: On which day does Arjun have 128 bacteria? (Express as 2ⁿ where 128 = 2ⁿ)
example.solution: Count: 2 = 2¹, 4 = 2², 8 = 2³, 16 = 2⁴, 32 = 2⁵, 64 = 2⁶, 128 = 2⁷. So 128 bacteria appear on day 7.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find the exponent that gives you the target number.

slides.title: The Multiplication Rule
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun her magic trick. 'What if I want to calculate 2³ × 2²? Instead of computing each separately, there's a shortcut.' She writes: 2³ × 2² = (2×2×2) × (2×2) = 2⁵. 'The exponents add!' Arjun grins. 'So I just add 3 and 2 to get 5?'
slides.inSimpleWords: When multiplying powers with the same base, add exponents.

slides.title: Laws of Exponents

points.label: Multiplication Rule
points.text: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (multiply: add exponents). E.g., 2³ × 2² = 2⁵ = 32

points.label: Division Rule
points.text: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (divide: subtract exponents). E.g., 2⁵ ÷ 2² = 2³ = 8

points.label: Power of Power
points.text: (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐˣⁿ (raise to power: multiply exponents). E.g., (2²)³ = 2⁶ = 64

slides.inSimpleWords: Rules make big exponent problems simpler.

image.alt: Laws of Exponents — Power Play

slides.title: Example 2: Applying Laws

example.problem: Simplify 3⁴ × 3². Then calculate the result.
example.solution: 3⁴ × 3² = 3⁴⁺² = 3⁶ = 729. Using the multiplication rule saves time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine exponents using the multiplication rule.

image.alt: Example 2: Applying Laws — Power Play

slides.title: Challenge 2: Division Rule

example.problem: Simplify 2⁷ ÷ 2³ using the division rule.
example.solution: 2⁷ ÷ 2³ = 2⁷⁻³ = 2⁴ = 16. The division rule lets you subtract exponents instead of dividing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use subtraction to divide powers of the same base.

slides.title: Power of Power
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks Priya, 'What if I square a square? Like, if I have 2² and I square it again?' Priya thinks: '(2²)² means (2²) × (2²) = 4 × 4 = 16. But there's a faster way: multiply the exponents. 2² × ² = 2⁴ = 16.' Arjun nods. 'Every rule saves time!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Power of power means multiply the exponents.

slides.title: Example 3: Power of Power

example.problem: Evaluate (3²)³ using the power-of-power rule.
example.solution: (3²)³ = 3²ˣ³ = 3⁶ = 729. Multiply exponents 2 × 3 to get 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you raise a power to a power, multiply exponents.

slides.title: Challenge 3: Mixed Laws

example.problem: Simplify (2³)² × 2¹ and evaluate.
example.solution: (2³)² = 2⁶. Then 2⁶ × 2¹ = 2⁷ = 128. First apply power-of-power, then multiplication rule.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine multiple exponent rules in one problem.

slides.title: Special Exponents
slides.storyContext: Arjun wonders: 'What about exponent 0? What about negative exponents?' Priya flips through her notebook. 'Good questions. 2⁰ = 1 — any nonzero number to power 0 is 1. And 2⁻¹ = 1/2, a negative exponent flips the fraction.' Arjun writes this down carefully.
slides.inSimpleWords: Exponent 0 gives 1; negative exponents are fractions.

slides.title: Special Cases

points.label: Exponent 1
points.text: a¹ = a. E.g., 5¹ = 5, 12¹ = 12. The exponent 1 doesn't change the number.

points.label: Negative Exponent
points.text: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. E.g., 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8. Negative flips to a fraction.

slides.inSimpleWords: Special exponents follow their own patterns.

slides.title: Example 4: Zero and Negative Exponents

example.problem: Evaluate 2⁰ and 2⁻² and 3⁰ × 2⁻¹.

slides.inSimpleWords: Special exponents have special values.

slides.title: Challenge 4: Apply All Rules

example.problem: Simplify (2³ × 2⁻¹) ÷ 2⁰.
example.solution: 2³ × 2⁻¹ = 2³⁺⁽⁻¹⁾ = 2² = 4. Then 2² ÷ 2⁰ = 2² ÷ 1 = 4. Any number ÷ 1 equals itself.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine multiplication, division, and special exponents.

slides.title: Big Numbers, Small Time
slides.storyContext: By the end of the week, Arjun's lab report is complete. The bacteria colony reaches 2¹⁰ = 1024 cells without needing a huge multiplication table. Priya says, 'That's the power of exponents. They let us express giant numbers compactly. Scientists use them for everything: atoms in a mole, stars in the universe, data storage capacity.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents let us write huge numbers simply.

slides.title: Real-World Use of Exponents

points.label: Science & Biology
points.text: Bacterial growth, viral spread, radioactive decay — all use exponential models.

points.label: Computer Science
points.text: Megabytes = 2²⁰ bytes, Gigabytes = 2³⁰ bytes. Storage capacity scales exponentially.

points.label: Finance
points.text: Compound interest uses exponents: A = P(1 + r)ᵗ. Money grows exponentially over time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents model real growth and scale.

slides.title: Example 5: Data Storage

example.problem: How many bytes are in 2 GB? (1 GB = 2³⁰ bytes)
example.solution: 2 GB = 2 × 2³⁰ bytes = 2¹ × 2³⁰ = 2³¹ bytes ≈ 2.1 billion bytes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Computer storage uses powers of 2.

slides.title: Challenge 5: Real Problem

example.problem: A virus infects 1 person, then 4 people, then 16, then 64. Express this as powers and find the pattern.
example.solution: Day 1: 4⁰ = 1. Day 2: 4¹ = 4. Day 3: 4² = 16. Day 4: 4³ = 64. Each day, the exponent increases by 1, and cases multiply by 4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponential spread happens faster than linear growth.

slides.title: Comparing Exponential and Linear Growth
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun a comparison graph. 'Look—if bacteria grew linearly (adding 2 each day), it'd be 2, 4, 6, 8, 10... after 10 days. But exponentially (multiplying by 2), it's 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024! Exponential beats linear by day 5.' Arjun realizes: 'This is why COVID spread so fast!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Exponential growth accelerates much faster than linear.

slides.title: Exponential vs. Linear Growth

points.label: Linear Growth
points.text: Add the same amount each time: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Slow, steady, predictable.

points.label: Exponential Growth
points.text: Multiply by the same factor each time: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Accelerating, explosive.

points.label: Real Examples
points.text: Bacteria double (exponential). Saving money with interest (exponential). Decay of radioactive material (exponential).

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponential growth accelerates rapidly.

slides.title: Challenge 6: Growth Comparison

example.problem: After 7 days, linear growth gives 14 (adding 2 each day). Exponential gives 2⁷ = 128. Which grows faster by day 10?
example.solution: Linear at day 10: 20 (adding 2 each day). Exponential: 2¹⁰ = 1024. Exponential is 51 times larger! Exponential always dominates in the long run.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponential growth beats linear growth every time.

slides.title: Power Play Summary

points.text: Exponents aⁿ replace repeated multiplication.
Laws of exponents simplify big calculations.
Arjun predicts bacteria; Priya predicts using powers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exponents make patterns and growth easy.

image.alt: Power Play Summary — Power Play

subject: Mathematics
title: Building Mumbai's Community Center
hook: Arjun's uncle is renovating a community center in Mumbai. He needs to choose between square, rectangular, and diamond-shaped plots. Priya explains the angle and side properties. Which shape is sturdiest?

slides.title: Choosing the Plot Shape
slides.storyContext: Arjun's uncle shows three land plots for the community center: one perfectly square, one rectangular, and one diamond-shaped (rhombus). 'Which is strongest?' he asks. Priya pulls out her geometry notes: 'It depends on their angles and sides. All quadrilaterals have 4 sides and angles summing to 360°.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Quadrilaterals are 4-sided closed figures.

image.alt: Choosing the Plot Shape — Quadrilaterals

slides.title: What is a Quadrilateral?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A quadrilateral is a polygon with exactly 4 sides and 4 angles.

points.label: Closed Figure
points.text: All sides connect to form a closed loop. No gaps, no intersections.

points.label: Common Examples
points.text: Squares, rectangles, rhombuses, trapezoids, parallelograms — all are quadrilaterals.

slides.inSimpleWords: A quadrilateral has 4 sides and 4 angles.

slides.title: Arjun's Angle Discovery
slides.storyContext: Arjun measures the angles on his uncle's three plots using Priya's protractor. Square: 90° + 90° + 90° + 90° = 360°. Rectangle: same! Diamond: 60° + 120° + 60° + 120° = 360°. 'Wait, they all add to 360°!' Arjun exclaims. Priya nods: 'That's the angle sum property of all quadrilaterals.'
slides.inSimpleWords: All quadrilateral angles sum to 360°.

slides.title: Angle Sum Property

points.label: Rule
points.text: Sum of all interior angles in any quadrilateral = 360°

points.label: Proof Context
points.text: Divide any quadrilateral into 2 triangles. Each triangle = 180°. Total = 360°.

points.label: Example
points.text: Rectangle: 90° + 90° + 90° + 90° = 360°. Diamond (rhombus): all 4 angles also sum to 360°.

slides.inSimpleWords: All 4 angles in a quadrilateral add to 360°.

image.alt: Angle Sum Property — Quadrilaterals

slides.title: Example 1: Finding Unknown Angle

example.problem: A quadrilateral has angles 80°, 100°, and 75°. Find the 4th angle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find missing angles using the 360° rule.

image.alt: Example 1: Finding Unknown Angle — Quadrilaterals

slides.title: Challenge 1: Angle Hunt

example.problem: A quadrilateral has three equal angles of 90° each. What is the 4th angle?
example.solution: 360° - (90° + 90° + 90°) = 360° - 270° = 90°. All four angles are 90°, so it's a rectangle or square.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the 360° rule to find any missing angle.

slides.title: Four Types of Quadrilaterals
slides.storyContext: Arjun's uncle decides to study each shape carefully. Priya draws four diagrams: a perfect square, a stretched rectangle, a tilted diamond, and a slanted four-sider. 'Look at their sides and angles. They're all different.' She explains how squares are special (all equal sides, all right angles), rectangles are flexible (opposite sides equal), and rhombuses and trapezoids have their own rules.
slides.inSimpleWords: Different quadrilaterals have different properties.

slides.title: Types of Quadrilaterals

points.label: Square
points.text: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles (90° each). Most stable for building.

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: Opposite sides equal, 4 right angles. Flexible length-to-width ratio.

points.label: Rhombus (Diamond)
points.text: 4 equal sides but angles NOT all 90°. Angles come in pairs (opposite angles equal).

points.label: Trapezium
points.text: One pair of parallel sides. Most irregular of the common types.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different quadrilaterals have different properties.

image.alt: Types of Quadrilaterals — Quadrilaterals

slides.title: Example 2: Rhombus Angles

example.problem: A rhombus plot has two angles of 60° each. Find the other two angles.
example.solution: In a rhombus, opposite angles are equal. If 2 angles = 60°, then 60° + 60° + ? + ? = 360°. The other two angles = (360° - 120°) ÷ 2 = 120° each.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rhombus has opposite angles that are equal.

image.alt: Example 2: Rhombus Angles — Quadrilaterals

slides.title: Challenge 2: Rectangle or Square?

example.problem: A plot has all 90° angles and all equal sides. What type of quadrilateral is it?
example.solution: A square. It has all right angles (rectangle property) AND all equal sides (rhombus property). When both are true, it's a square.

slides.inSimpleWords: A square combines rectangle and rhombus properties.

slides.title: Opposite Sides and Angles
slides.storyContext: Priya explains a key property: 'In a parallelogram—and rhombuses are special parallelograms—opposite sides are parallel and opposite angles are equal.' Arjun draws this: 'So if one angle is 70°, its opposite is also 70°?' 'Exactly,' Priya confirms. 'And the other two angles are both 110°, since 70° + 110° = 180°.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite sides and angles have matching properties.

slides.title: Parallelogram Properties

points.label: Opposite Sides Equal
points.text: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal in length and parallel.

points.label: Opposite Angles Equal
points.text: In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal. Angles on the same side sum to 180°.

points.label: Diagonals
points.text: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other (cross at midpoints).

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallelograms have matching opposite sides and angles.

slides.title: Example 3: Parallelogram Angles

example.problem: A parallelogram plot has one angle of 75°. Find all four angles.
example.solution: Opposite angle = 75° (opposite angles equal). Adjacent angles = 180° - 75° = 105° each. So angles are: 75°, 105°, 75°, 105°.

slides.inSimpleWords: One angle determines all others in a parallelogram.

slides.title: Challenge 3: Diagonal Bisection

example.problem: In a parallelogram, one diagonal is divided into segments of 5 cm and 5 cm at the crossing point. What is the other diagonal's length at its crossing point?
example.solution: Since diagonals bisect each other, each half of the crossing diagonal is 5 cm. The full length is 10 cm. (Each half is equal length.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Diagonals split equally at their intersection.

slides.title: Trapezium: The Unique One
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks about the trapezium shape. Priya explains: 'A trapezium has only ONE pair of parallel sides, unlike a parallelogram which has TWO pairs. This makes it less stable for building, but useful for other designs.' She shows him examples from Indian architecture where trapezium shapes appear.
slides.inSimpleWords: Trapeziums have only one pair of parallel sides.

slides.title: Trapezium and Other Quadrilaterals

points.label: Trapezium
points.text: Exactly one pair of parallel sides. Angles don't have simple relationships like parallelograms.

points.label: Kite
points.text: Two pairs of adjacent equal sides. Diagonals perpendicular. Only one pair of opposite angles equal.

points.label: Irregular Quadrilateral
points.text: No parallel sides, no equal sides. Only guaranteed property: angles sum to 360°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Other quadrilaterals have unique properties.

slides.title: Example 4: Trapezium Angles

example.problem: A trapezium has angles 50°, 130°, 70°. Find the 4th angle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Any quadrilateral angles sum to 360°.

slides.title: Challenge 4: Real Building Decision

example.problem: Arjun's uncle must choose: square (all sides 10m, all angles 90°) or rectangle (10m × 15m, all angles 90°). Which encloses more area for the community center?
example.solution: Square area = 10 × 10 = 100 m². Rectangle area = 10 × 15 = 150 m². Rectangle encloses more but uses more materials. Depends on the budget.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different shapes enclose different areas.

slides.title: The Perfect Choice
slides.storyContext: After studying all types, Arjun's uncle decides: 'The main building is square (strongest, equal sides), but the courtyard will be rectangular (flexible, fits the street boundary). The rhombus will be decorative (beautiful angles).' Priya smiles. 'Each shape serves its purpose. Understanding their properties helps you choose wisely.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Different quadrilaterals suit different purposes.

slides.title: Perimeter and Area Basics

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Sum of all four sides. Square with side 10m: 10+10+10+10 = 40m. Rectangle 10×15: 10+15+10+15 = 50m.

points.label: Area of Square
points.text: side². Square with side 10m: 10² = 100 m².

points.label: Area of Rectangle
points.text: length × width. Rectangle 10m × 15m: 10 × 15 = 150 m².

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is around; area is inside.

slides.title: Example 5: Building Plot Comparison

example.problem: A square plot costs Rs 500/m² and a rectangular plot costs Rs 400/m². Square is 20m on each side; rectangle is 20m × 30m. Which is more expensive?
example.solution: Square area: 20² = 400 m². Cost: 400 × 500 = Rs 2,00,000. Rectangle area: 20 × 30 = 600 m². Cost: 600 × 400 = Rs 2,40,000. Rectangle is more expensive but larger.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare area and cost for practical decisions.

slides.title: Challenge 5: Complete Plot Design

example.problem: A plot must be rectangular, 20m long. If the builder wants 300 m² area, what should the width be? What's the perimeter?
example.solution: Area = length × width. 300 = 20 × width. Width = 15m. Perimeter = 20+15+20+15 = 70m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use formulas to find missing dimensions.

slides.title: Symmetry in Quadrilaterals
slides.storyContext: Arjun notices something beautiful. 'The square looks the same from every angle. But the rectangle only looks the same if you flip it sideways.' Priya nods: 'That's symmetry. Squares have 4-fold rotational symmetry; rectangles have 2-fold. Rhombuses also have 2-fold. Symmetry makes shapes beautiful AND strong.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry is a hidden property of shapes.

slides.title: Symmetry in Quadrilaterals

points.label: Line Symmetry
points.text: Mirror reflection through a line. Square has 4 lines of symmetry. Rectangle has 2. Rhombus has 2.

points.label: Rotational Symmetry
points.text: Shape looks same after rotation. Square: 90° rotation. Rectangle: 180°. Trapezium: usually none.

points.label: Architectural Use
points.text: Symmetrical designs are aesthetically pleasing and structurally balanced.

slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry reveals hidden geometry.

slides.title: Quadrilaterals Overview

points.text: All quadrilaterals have 4 sides and angles summing to 360°.
Squares and rectangles are most stable for construction.
Each type has unique angle and side properties.

slides.inSimpleWords: Quadrilaterals are essential shapes in building.

image.alt: Quadrilaterals Overview — Quadrilaterals

subject: Mathematics
title: The School Lunch Mystery
hook: The school lunch manager in Delhi needs to divide 144 chapatis equally among students. Priya and Arjun discover divisibility shortcuts: 144 is even (divisible by 2), sums digits to 9 (divisible by 9). How many ways can they divide the chapatis?

slides.title: Dividing Lunch Equally
slides.storyContext: The school has 144 chapatis to serve for lunch. The manager asks: 'Can I divide them equally among 8 students? Among 9? Among 5?' Priya flips through her number tricks notebook: 'Let me check the divisibility rules. 144 ends in 4, so it's even (divisible by 2). Add digits: 1+4+4=9, divisible by 9!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility rules find factors without dividing.

image.alt: Dividing Lunch Equally — Number Play

slides.title: What is Divisibility?

points.label: Simple Definition
points.text: A number is divisible by another if it divides evenly with no remainder. 8 is divisible by 2 (8÷2=4, no remainder).

points.label: Factor
points.text: If a divides b evenly, then a is a factor (or divisor) of b. Factors help us find all ways to divide a number.

points.label: Why It Matters
points.text: Finding factors quickly lets us solve word problems (like dividing chapatis) without actual division.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility tells if one number divides another evenly.

slides.title: The Shortcut Discovery
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks, 'Do I need to actually divide 144 by every number to check? That's slow.' Priya shows him her notebook: 'Rules! Every digit divisible by 2 ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. Every number whose digits sum to 3 (or 9) is divisible by 3 (or 9). Shortcuts save time.' Arjun's eyes widen. 'This is like cheating, but math-allowed!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility rules are quick shortcuts.

slides.title: Divisibility Rules

points.label: Divisibility by 2
points.text: Number ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. E.g., 144 ends in 4 → divisible by 2.

points.label: Divisibility by 3
points.text: Sum of digits is divisible by 3. E.g., 144: 1+4+4=9 (divisible by 3) → 144 divisible by 3.

points.label: Divisibility by 9
points.text: Sum of digits is divisible by 9. E.g., 144: 1+4+4=9 → divisible by 9.

points.label: Divisibility by 5
points.text: Number ends in 0 or 5. E.g., 145 ends in 5 → divisible by 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Quick tricks test if numbers divide evenly.

image.alt: Divisibility Rules — Number Play

slides.title: Example 1: Chapati Division

example.problem: Check if 144 chapatis can be divided equally among 9 students.
example.solution: Use divisibility by 9: sum of digits = 1+4+4 = 9. Since 9 is divisible by 9, 144 is divisible by 9. Each student gets 144÷9 = 16 chapatis.

slides.inSimpleWords: 144 divided by 9 gives exactly 16 per student.

image.alt: Example 1: Chapati Division — Number Play

slides.title: Challenge 1: Divisibility Check

example.problem: Is 240 divisible by 5? Is it divisible by 3? By 9?
example.solution: By 5: ends in 0 → YES. By 3: 2+4+0=6 (divisible by 3) → YES. By 9: 6 is not divisible by 9 → NO.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply each rule to find divisibility quickly.

slides.title: Prime vs Composite
slides.storyContext: Arjun wonders: 'Can I break down every number into smaller factors? Or are some numbers special?' Priya explains: 'Some numbers have only 2 factors: 1 and themselves. We call them primes. Others have many factors. Those are composite. It's like some numbers are building blocks; others are made FROM blocks.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Numbers are either prime or composite.

slides.title: Prime vs. Composite

points.label: Prime Number
points.text: A number with exactly 2 factors: 1 and itself. E.g., 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 are prime.

points.label: Composite Number
points.text: A number with more than 2 factors. E.g., 4 (factors: 1,2,4), 6 (factors: 1,2,3,6), 144 (many factors).

points.label: 1 is Special
points.text: 1 has only 1 factor (itself), so it's neither prime nor composite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Primes have 2 factors; composites have more.

image.alt: Prime vs. Composite — Number Play

slides.title: Example 2: Prime Check

example.problem: Is 17 a prime number? List all its factors.
example.solution: Factors of 17: 1 and 17 only. Since it has exactly 2 factors, 17 is prime. (No other number divides 17 evenly.)

slides.inSimpleWords: 17 is prime because only 1 and 17 divide it.

image.alt: Example 2: Prime Check — Number Play

slides.title: Challenge 2: Identify the Type

example.problem: Is 20 prime or composite? List all its factors.
example.solution: Factors of 20: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20. That's 6 factors (more than 2), so 20 is composite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count factors to decide prime vs. composite.

slides.title: Finding All Factors
slides.storyContext: Priya continues: 'To divide 144 chapatis fairly, I need ALL ways to split them. That means finding every factor. 144 = 1×144, 2×72, 3×48, 4×36, 6×24, 8×18, 9×16, 12×12. Each pair tells us how to divide.' Arjun realizes: 'So there are 15 different ways to divide them!'
slides.inSimpleWords: All factor pairs show ways to divide a number.

slides.title: Finding All Factors

points.label: Factor Pairs
points.text: If a × b = n, then a and b are a factor pair of n. For 144: 1×144, 2×72, 3×48, etc.

points.label: Systematic Method
points.text: Start with 1 and n. Then check 2, 3, 4... up to √n. When you find a factor, its pair automatically exists.

points.label: Purpose
points.text: Factor pairs help in division problems, simplifying fractions, finding GCD and LCM.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every factor has a pair that multiplies to the number.

slides.title: Example 3: Factor Pairs

example.problem: Find all factors of 24.
example.solution: Pairs: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6. So all factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 (8 factors total).

slides.inSimpleWords: List all factor pairs to find all factors.

slides.title: Challenge 3: Factor Hunt

example.problem: How many ways can 36 chapatis be divided among students (equal per student)? List all possibilities.
example.solution: Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Each represents a group size: 36 groups of 1, 18 groups of 2, 12 groups of 3, 9 groups of 4, 6 groups of 6, 4 groups of 9, 3 groups of 12, 2 groups of 18, 1 group of 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each factor shows one way to divide.

slides.title: GCD and LCM
slides.storyContext: The manager asks a tricky question: 'If I have 144 chapatis and 120 cookies, how can I divide them into equal boxes with no leftovers?' Priya explains: 'Find the GCD—Greatest Common Divisor. 144 and 120 both divide by 24. So we make 6 boxes with 24 chapatis and 5 cookies each.' Arjun nods: 'One tool, multiple problems!'
slides.inSimpleWords: GCD helps divide multiple quantities fairly.

slides.title: GCD and LCM Basics

points.label: GCD (Greatest Common Divisor)
points.text: Largest number that divides both numbers evenly. GCD(144, 120) = 24. Useful for fair division.

points.label: LCM (Least Common Multiple)
points.text: Smallest number divisible by both. LCM(12, 18) = 36. Useful for syncing cycles.

points.label: Finding GCD
points.text: List factors of both numbers; pick the largest common one. Or use Euclidean algorithm for bigger numbers.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD and LCM solve real-world grouping problems.

slides.title: Example 4: GCD Application

example.problem: Find GCD(36, 48). Use it to arrange items into equal boxes.
example.solution: Factors of 36: 1,2,3,4,6,9,12,18,36. Factors of 48: 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,16,24,48. GCD = 12. So make 12 boxes: 3 items of type A, 4 items of type B per box.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD is the largest common factor.

slides.title: Challenge 4: GCD Problem

example.problem: A bakery has 60 cookies and 80 cupcakes. What's the largest number of identical boxes they can fill with no remainder?

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD finds the largest equal-group size.

slides.title: Prime Factorization
slides.storyContext: Priya explains another trick: 'Every composite number can be broken into prime factors. 144 = 2⁴ × 3². These are the building blocks—the primes that multiply to give 144.' Arjun tries: '12 = 2² × 3. That's neat—primes are like Lego blocks for all numbers!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every number is made from prime factors.

slides.title: Prime Factorization

points.label: Definition
points.text: Expressing a number as a product of prime numbers. E.g., 144 = 2⁴ × 3² = 16 × 9.

points.label: Prime Factorization Process
points.text: Divide by smallest primes (2, 3, 5, 7...) repeatedly until you reach 1. All composite numbers have unique factorization.

points.label: Purpose
points.text: Finding GCD, LCM, simplifying fractions, understanding number structure.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break numbers into their prime building blocks.

slides.title: Example 5: Prime Factorization

example.problem: Find the prime factorization of 60.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide repeatedly by primes to factorize.

slides.title: Challenge 5: Factorization Chain

example.problem: Prime factorize 72 and 48. Use them to find GCD(72,48).
example.solution: 72 = 2³ × 3². 48 = 2⁴ × 3. Common factors: 2³ × 3 = 8 × 3 = 24. So GCD = 24.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime factors help find GCD easily.

slides.title: Real-World Number Secrets
slides.storyContext: Priya concludes: 'Numbers hide patterns everywhere. Primes protect your passwords (RSA encryption uses large primes). Divisibility rules save time in accounting. GCD/LCM solve real problems: scheduling buses, dividing resources. Math isn't abstract—it's practical magic.' Arjun smiles. 'The lunch mystery revealed the power of numbers!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Number properties solve real-world problems.

slides.title: Challenge 6: Complete Number Detective

example.problem: A number is divisible by both 6 and 8. Is it divisible by 24? What's the LCM(6,8)?
example.solution: If divisible by both 6 and 8, it's divisible by LCM(6,8). 6=2×3, 8=2³. LCM=2³×3=24. Yes, it's divisible by 24. LCM tells the smallest common multiple.

slides.inSimpleWords: LCM finds the smallest common multiple.

slides.title: Number Play Summary

points.text: Divisibility rules save time without actual division.
Prime numbers have exactly 2 factors; composites have more.
144 chapatis divide equally—Priya solved it with rules.

slides.inSimpleWords: Number tricks reveal hidden factors.

image.alt: Number Play Summary — Number Play

subject: Mathematics
title: Recipe Scaling for a School Festival
hook: Priya's mother makes a kheer (rice pudding) for 4 people using 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee. For 20 people at the school festival, how much of each ingredient? Arjun uses ratios to scale the recipe perfectly.

slides.title: Scaling the Festival Kheer
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother's kheer recipe serves 4 people: 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee. The school festival expects 20 people. 'Do I just add more randomly?' she asks. Arjun says: 'No! Scale using ratios. The recipe must stay in the same proportion.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Proportions scale recipes and measurements.

image.alt: Scaling the Festival Kheer — Proportional Reasoning-1

slides.title: The Festival Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun brainstorm in the kitchen. Priya says: 'If I just double everything, will it work?' Arjun shakes his head: '4 people becomes 20? That's not double, that's five times!' They write it down: 4 × scale factor = 20. Scale factor = 5. Every ingredient gets multiplied by 5—not more, not less.
slides.inSimpleWords: To scale a recipe, find how many times bigger it needs to be.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A ratio compares two quantities. Rice : Milk = 1 : 2 means for every 1 cup rice, use 2 cups milk.

points.label: Notation
points.text: Write as 1:2, 1/2, or '1 to 2'. All mean the same comparison.

points.label: Everyday Examples
points.text: Recipe ratios (1:2), map ratios (1:1000000), probability (3:5 for winning odds).

points.label: Same Ratio, Different Numbers
points.text: 1:2 (1 rice : 2 milk), 2:4 (2 rice : 4 milk), 5:10 (5 rice : 10 milk)—all taste identical.

points.label: Cross-Multiplication Check
points.text: For ratios a:b and c:d, if a×d = b×c, they are equivalent. E.g., 1×4 = 2×2 ✓

points.label: Simplest Form
points.text: Reduce 10:20 by dividing both by 10 → 1:2. Simplest form is clearest.

slides.title: Example 1: Scaling Kheer

example.problem: Scale the kheer recipe for 20 people. Original (4 people): 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee.
example.solution: Scale factor = 20÷4 = 5. New recipe: 1×5 = 5 cups rice, 2×5 = 10 cups milk, 3×5 = 15 tbsp ghee.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply all ingredients by the scale factor.

image.alt: Example 1: Scaling Kheer — Proportional Reasoning-1

slides.title: Priya Tests the Scaled Recipe
slides.storyContext: They make the festival kheer using the scaled amounts: 5 cups rice, 10 cups milk, 15 tbsp ghee. The first batch feeds exactly 20 people. Priya tastes it: 'It's perfect! The ratio stayed the same, so it tastes just like Amma's small-batch version.'

example.problem: Original recipe serves 4. Half-recipe for 2 people: 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee.
example.solution: Scale factor = 2÷4 = 0.5. Divide all: 1×0.5 = 0.5 cup rice, 2×0.5 = 1 cup milk, 3×0.5 = 1.5 tbsp ghee.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Scale factor = New amount ÷ Original amount. For 4 → 20 people: 20÷4 = 5.

points.label: Scaling Up
points.text: If scale factor > 1, recipe grows. If < 1, recipe shrinks.

points.label: Checking Your Work
points.text: Original × scale factor = new. Check: 4×5 = 20 ✓

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two quantities are directly proportional if as one increases, the other increases at the same rate.

points.label: Constant Ratio Test
points.text: If x and y are directly proportional, x:y is always the same. E.g., 1 rice : 2 milk stays 5 rice : 10 milk.

points.label: Formula
points.text: y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality. E.g., milk = 2 × rice.

image.alt: Direct Proportion — Proportional Reasoning-1

slides.title: Arjun Discovers the Pattern
slides.storyContext: At the festival, Arjun writes down quantities for 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 people. He notices: rice is always half the milk amount. No matter the scale, rice:milk stays 1:2. 'This is the constant!' he says. 'The formula is milk = 2 × rice.'

points.label: What is k?
points.text: k is the number you multiply by to go from one quantity to another. For kheer: k = 2 (milk = 2 × rice).

points.label: Finding k
points.text: Divide one quantity by the other: k = y÷x. E.g., 10 cups milk ÷ 5 cups rice = 2.

points.label: Using k
points.text: Once you know k, predict any value: If 30 people, rice = 30÷4 = 7.5 cups, milk = 7.5 × 2 = 15 cups.

example.problem: If 3 notebooks cost Rs 60, what do 7 notebooks cost? (Assuming direct proportion.)
example.solution: Cost per notebook k = 60÷3 = Rs 20. Cost of 7 notebooks = 7×20 = Rs 140.

points.label: Straight Line Through Origin
points.text: Plot people vs. rice cups: (4,1), (8,2), (12,3), (20,5). Points line up through (0,0).

points.label: Slope = Constant k
points.text: Rise÷Run = 1÷4 = 0.25. The slope tells k: rice = 0.25 × people.

points.label: No Recipe = No Ingredients
points.text: At 0 people, 0 rice, 0 milk. Direct proportion always crosses origin.

slides.title: Not Everything Scales Proportionally
slides.storyContext: Later, Arjun asks: 'Does cooking time scale the same way?' Grandpa says no. 'Doubling kheer doesn't double cooking time. Some things are proportional, some aren't. Always check the real world.'

example.problem: A recipe uses 1 cup flour for 4 cookies. Does 2 cups flour make 8 cookies? Oven time also matters.
example.solution: More ingredients ≠ proportionally more cookies if baking time stays same. If you double flour but bake for same time, cookies burn or underbake. Not directly proportional.

example.problem: Original kheer (4 people): 1 cup rice, 2 cups milk, 3 tbsp ghee. If Priya makes it for 10 people, what are the new amounts?
example.solution: Scale factor = 10÷4 = 2.5. Rice: 1×2.5 = 2.5 cups. Milk: 2×2.5 = 5 cups. Ghee: 3×2.5 = 7.5 tbsp.

example.problem: Arjun needs 20 cups milk for the festival. Original recipe has 2 cups milk for 4 people. How many people will this serve?
example.solution: Scale factor = 20÷2 = 10. So original 4 × 10 = 40 people. Check: 4 → 10× scale → 40 people, 2 cups milk → 10× → 20 cups. ✓

example.problem: 10 cups rice to 20 cups milk. Simplify the ratio and find the constant k.
example.solution: 10:20 = 1:2 (divide both by 10). k = 2 (milk = 2 × rice).

points.label: Not Always Direct
points.text: Some quantities are inversely proportional: as one increases, the other decreases. E.g., workers vs. time to finish job.

points.label: Formula Difference
points.text: Direct: y = kx. Inverse: y = k/x (constant divided by x).

points.label: Example
points.text: 10 workers finish job in 5 days. 5 workers finish in 10 days. 50 = 10×5 = 5×10. Constant k = 50.

example.problem: A festival cooking team needs to make 100 kg kheer. 4 cooks take 8 hours. How long for 2 cooks?
example.solution: Inverse: workers × hours = constant. 4×8 = 32. So 2×h = 32. h = 16 hours. Fewer workers = more time.

points.label: Recipes & Cooking
points.text: Scale ingredients by serving size. Direct proportion.

points.label: Maps & Distance
points.text: 1:1000000 scale on map. 1 cm = 1000000 cm (10 km) on ground. Direct proportion.

points.label: Money & Shopping
points.text: Cost = quantity × price/unit. Direct proportion with price constant.

example.problem: A map of Punjab uses scale 1:500000. The distance from Amritsar to Ludhiana on map is 8 cm. What is actual distance?
example.solution: Actual distance = map distance × scale factor. 8 cm × 500000 = 4000000 cm = 40 km.

points.label: Method 1: Constant Ratio
points.text: For each pair, calculate ratio. If all ratios equal, quantities are proportional. 4:2, 8:4, 12:6 all = 2:1 ✓

points.label: Method 2: Cross-Multiply
points.text: For pairs (a,b) and (c,d): if a×d = b×c, they're proportional. 4×4 = 2×8 ✓ (both = 16)

points.label: Method 3: Graph
points.text: Plot points on graph. If they form a straight line through origin, quantities are directly proportional.

slides.title: The Festival Success
slides.storyContext: Festival day arrives. Priya and Arjun serve 100+ guests using their ratio knowledge. Grandpa watches them measure perfectly. 'You both learned that proportions are everywhere—cooking, budgets, maps, everything scales with ratios.'

slides.title: Proportional Reasoning

points.text: Ratios compare quantities; equivalent ratios stay proportional.
Scale factor multiplies or divides all quantities equally.
Direct proportion: y = kx (constant k). Always a straight line through origin.
Not everything scales—always verify with real-world observations.

slides.inSimpleWords: Proportions scale recipes and prices perfectly.

image.alt: Proportional Reasoning — Proportional Reasoning-1

subject: Mathematics
title: Cricket Scores and Batting Averages
hook: Arjun watches an Indian cricket match. The batter has a batting average of 0.75 (three hits in four attempts). Is that the same as ¾? Priya shows him how decimals, fractions, and percentages are all the same number dressed up differently.

slides.title: Fractions in Disguise: Three Forms of One Number
Batting Average Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun watches the IPL (Indian Premier League) match on TV. Commentator says: 'Batter's average this season: 0.75.' Arjun wonders: 'Is that good?' Priya says: '0.75 = ¾ = 75%. That means 3 hits out of every 4 attempts. Pretty good for cricket!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Decimals, fractions, and percentages are the same.

image.alt: Batting Average Mystery — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: The Three Disguises
slides.storyContext: Arjun is confused. Priya draws three columns on paper: Fraction (¾), Decimal (0.75), Percentage (75%). 'Same person, three outfits,' she laughs. 'The batter succeeds ¾ of the time, or 0.75 (out of 1.0), or 75% (out of 100). They're triplets, not strangers.'

points.label: Parts and Wholes
points.text: Fraction = numerator (top) ÷ denominator (bottom). ¾ means 3 parts out of 4 equal parts.

points.label: What Denominator Means
points.text: Denominator = how many equal parts the whole is divided into. ¾: the whole is cut into 4 pieces.

points.label: What Numerator Means
points.text: Numerator = how many of those pieces you have. ¾: you have 3 of the 4 pieces.

points.label: The Conversion
points.text: Divide numerator by denominator. ¾ = 3÷4 = 0.75

points.label: Long Division Method
points.text: ⅝: 5÷8 = 0.625. Put decimal, divide: 50÷8=6 rem 2, 20÷8=2 rem 4, 40÷8=5. Result: 0.625.

points.label: Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths
points.text: 0.75: 7 in tenths place (0.7), 5 in hundredths place (0.05). 0.75 = 0.7 + 0.05.

points.label: Reading Decimals
points.text: 0.75 is 'zero point seven five' or 'seventy-five hundredths'. Think of it as a fraction: 75/100.

points.label: Decimal to Fraction
points.text: 0.75 = 75/100. Then simplify using GCD: 75/100 = ¾.

example.problem: A cricketer hits 5 fours in 8 deliveries. Express as fraction, decimal, and percentage.
example.solution: Fraction: ⅝. Decimal: 5÷8 = 0.625. Percentage: 0.625 × 100 = 62.5%. All three express the same batting success.

image.alt: Example 1: Cricket Batting Average — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Arjun Checks His Cricket Stats
slides.storyContext: Arjun looks at his own practice stats: 6 successful runs out of 10. Priya helps: '6/10 = 0.6 = 60%. You're 60% successful. If you practice more, can you hit 75% like the pro?'

points.label: Percent Means Hundredths
points.text: 'Per cent' = per hundred. 75% = 75/100 = 0.75.

points.label: Converting Decimal to Percent
points.text: Multiply by 100: 0.75 × 100 = 75%. Or move decimal 2 places right: 0.75 → 75.

points.label: Converting Percent to Decimal
points.text: Divide by 100: 75% ÷ 100 = 0.75. Or move decimal 2 places left: 75 → 0.75.

points.label: Step 1: Count Decimal Places
points.text: 0.75 has 2 decimal places → put over 100. 0.625 has 3 decimal places → put over 1000.

points.label: Prime Factorization
points.text: 75 = 3×5². 100 = 2²×5². Common factors: 5². So GCD = 5×5 = 25.

points.label: Then Simplify
points.text: Divide both numerator and denominator by GCD: 75÷25=3, 100÷25=4. Result: ¾.

example.problem: Express 40% as a fraction in simplest form.

image.alt: Example 2: Percentage to Fraction — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Simplifying Arjun's Stats
slides.storyContext: Arjun's average: 20 hits in 80 attempts. Priya simplifies: '20/80 = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. Easier to remember—you're 25% successful. Work on your technique!'

points.label: What They Are
points.text: Some fractions give non-ending decimals. ⅓ = 0.333... (3 repeats forever).

points.label: Notation
points.text: Write a bar over repeating digits: 0.3̄ (means 0.333...), 0.16̄ (means 0.1666...).

points.label: Which Fractions Repeat?
points.text: Denominators 3,6,7,9,11... give repeating. Denominators 2,4,5,10... give terminating (ending).

example.problem: Convert 0.333... (repeating) to a fraction.
example.solution: 0.333... = ⅓. Check: 1÷3 = 0.333... ✓. Decimals that repeat often hide fractions with 3,6,7,9 in denominator.

points.label: Marking Key Points
points.text: 0, ¼ (0.25), ½ (0.5), ¾ (0.75), 1 equally spaced on a line.

points.label: Ordering Numbers
points.text: 0.6 = ⅗ lies between ½ (0.5) and ¾ (0.75). Helps compare and order values.

points.label: Mixed Numbers
points.text: 1¼ = 1.25, 1⅖ = 1.4. Improper fraction 7/5 = 1.4 on the line.

example.problem: A batsman scores 3 centuries in 12 matches. Write as fraction, decimal, and percentage.
example.solution: Fraction: 3/12 = ¼ (simplified). Decimal: 0.25. Percentage: 25%.

example.problem: Order from smallest to largest: 0.6, ⅗, 62%, 0.602
example.solution: Convert all to decimals: 0.6, 0.6, 0.62, 0.602. Order: ⅗ and 0.6 (tied), 0.602, then 0.62 (largest).

example.problem: Simplify 30/45 and convert to decimal and percent.
example.solution: GCD(30,45)=15. Simplify: 30÷15=2, 45÷15=3. So 30/45 = ⅔. Decimal: 2÷3 = 0.666... Percent: 66.67% (approximately).

points.label: Improper Fractions
points.text: Numerator ≥ denominator. E.g., 7/4 (means 7 parts, but only 4 in a whole). Greater than or equal to 1.

points.label: Mixed Numbers
points.text: Whole number + fraction. 7/4 = 1¾ (one whole, plus ¾ more).

points.label: Conversion
points.text: 7÷4 = 1 remainder 3. So 7/4 = 1¾. Reverse: 1¾ = (1×4+3)/4 = 7/4.

example.problem: Convert 13/5 to a mixed number.

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: ¼ + ¾ = (1+3)/4 = 4/4 = 1. Just add numerators.

points.label: Different Denominators
points.text: ½ + ⅓: Find common denominator (LCD). LCD(2,3)=6. ½=3/6, ⅓=2/6. 3/6+2/6=5/6.

points.label: Finding LCD
points.text: Multiples of 2: 2,4,6,8... Multiples of 3: 3,6,9... Least common = 6.

example.problem: A cricketer bats in 3 innings: scores ⅓, ¼, ⅕ of total runs. What fraction of total in all three?

points.label: Multiplication
points.text: ½ × ⅔ = (1×2)/(2×3) = 2/6 = ⅓. Numerator×numerator, denominator×denominator.

points.label: Division
points.text: ½ ÷ ⅔ = ½ × 3/2 = 3/4. Flip second fraction (reciprocal), then multiply.

points.label: Reciprocal
points.text: ⅔ flips to 3/2. Any fraction's reciprocal: swap numerator and denominator.

slides.title: The Tournament Results
slides.storyContext: Arjun practices daily. His average improves: 12 hits in 16 attempts → 12/16 = ¾ = 0.75 = 75%. He shows Priya his scorecard. 'You did it! You hit the pro's average!' Priya smiles. 'Now you understand: ¾, 0.75, 75%—they're the same champion.'

slides.title: Fractions in Disguise

points.text: Fractions (¾), decimals (0.75), and percentages (75%) express the same value.
Convert by dividing (fraction→decimal) or using powers of 10 (decimal→fraction).
Simplify fractions using GCD to see the clearest form.
Some fractions repeat (⅓ = 0.333...), others terminate (¼ = 0.25).

slides.inSimpleWords: One number, three different disguises.

image.alt: Fractions in Disguise — Fractions in Disguise

subject: Science
title: Priya's Organic Farm in Punjab
hook: Priya's grandparents run an organic farm near Amritsar, Punjab. They grow wheat and rice using rotation, composting, and natural pest control. How do crop selection, soil quality, and water management make farming successful?

slides.title: Crop Production and Management: Farm Wisdom
Grandpa's Wheat Field
slides.storyContext: Priya visits the Punjab farm during harvest. Golden wheat fields stretch for acres. 'Grandpa, how do you keep this soil so rich year after year?' Baldev smiles: 'We rotate crops—wheat one year, legumes next. We compost, we let the land rest. The soil is living.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Good farming needs planning, soil care, and rotation.

image.alt: Grandpa's Wheat Field — Crop Production and Management

slides.title: The Soil Test
slides.storyContext: Priya and Grandpa Baldev dig into the black soil. 'See these worms and insects? They're farmers too—breaking down dead leaves, making nutrients available.' He crumbles a handful: 'This texture, this color—it took decades of organic practice to build. Chemical farming would have killed it.'

points.label: Nutrients (NPK)
points.text: Crops need Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Potassium (K). Ratios vary by crop. Wheat needs high N; legumes add N to soil.

points.label: Water Management
points.text: Irrigation timing is critical. Wheat in Punjab: rabi crop (winter); rice: kharif (monsoon). Wrong water timing = crop failure.

points.label: Light & Temperature
points.text: Wheat thrives in cool season. Rice in warm, monsoon season. Altitude and latitude affect crop choice.

points.label: Nitrogen (N) — The Leafy Nutrient
points.text: Makes plants green, promotes leaf & stem growth. Deficiency: pale leaves, stunted growth. Wheat & corn are hungry for N.

points.label: Phosphorus (P) — Root & Flower Builder
points.text: Aids root growth, flower & fruit development. Deficiency: weak roots, poor crops. Critical for legume pods.

points.label: Potassium (K) — Disease Fighter
points.text: Strengthens plant immunity, improves water retention. Deficiency: weak stems, disease-prone. Needed by fruits & tubers.

example.problem: Grandpa grows wheat (high N demand) year 1. What should he grow year 2 to restore nitrogen?
example.solution: Grow legumes (chickpea, peas, clover). They have nitrogen-fixing bacteria in roots that add N to soil. Year 3: wheat again, with richer soil.

image.alt: Example 1: Crop Rotation — Crop Production and Management

slides.title: Legumes to the Rescue
slides.storyContext: Year 2, Grandpa plants chickpeas where wheat grew. Priya asks: 'Why chickpeas after wheat?' He explains: 'Chickpeas have root nodules with special bacteria—they pull nitrogen from the air and lock it in the soil. Free fertilizer! In year 3, the soil is restored.'

points.label: Rabi (Winter) Crops
points.text: Wheat, mustard, peas planted Oct-Nov after monsoon. Need winter rain or canal irrigation. Harvest Feb-Mar.

points.label: Kharif (Monsoon) Crops
points.text: Rice, maize, cotton planted Jun-Jul when monsoon rains start. Heavy water needs from nature. Harvest Sep-Oct.

points.label: Zaid (Summer) Crops
points.text: Watermelon, cucumber, pumpkin planted Mar-Apr. Short season, needs irrigation. Harvest Jun-Jul.

points.label: Too Much Water
points.text: Waterlogging, root rot, fungal disease. Soil must drain well; fields need canals or drains.

points.label: Too Little Water
points.text: Drought stress, wilting, poor yield. Crops need consistent moisture, not flooding then dry.

points.label: Timing Matters
points.text: Wheat needs 4-5 irrigation cycles: Nov-Dec, Jan (tillering), Feb (boot), Mar (grain fill). Skip if winter rains are good.

example.problem: Grandpa grows rabi wheat planted Oct 15. Monsoon ends; soil moisture drops. When to irrigate?
example.solution: Wheat needs critical stages: Nov-Dec (if dry), Jan (tillering), Feb (boot stage), Mar (grain fill). Too early = waterlogging; too late = drought stress.

points.label: Tilling & Mulching
points.text: Loosen soil before planting (tilling). Mulch (straw, leaves) retains moisture, blocks weeds, prevents erosion.

points.label: Compost Making
points.text: Layer farm waste: dried leaves, crop residue, kitchen scraps. Add water, let decompose 3-6 months. Golden brown = ready.

points.label: Manure & Organic Matter
points.text: Cow/poultry manure is organic fertilizer. Improves soil texture, water-holding capacity, microbial activity.

example.problem: Grandpa has wheat straw, cow dung, and vegetable scraps. Make compost for next year's soil.
example.solution: Layer: straw (carbon) + cow dung (nitrogen + microbes) + water. Repeat layers. Turn every 2 weeks. In 4 months, dark crumbly compost. Mix 2-3 tons into soil before planting.

points.label: Beneficial Insects
points.text: Ladybugs eat aphids, parasitic wasps kill caterpillars, ground beetles eat slugs. Attract them with flowers (marigold, sunflower).

points.label: Neem & Organic Sprays
points.text: Neem oil (2% in water) targets aphids/mites without harming bees or microbes. Spray every 7-10 days during pest season.

points.label: Crop Rotation & Intercropping
points.text: Rotate crops to break pest cycles. Intercrop (maize+beans) confuses pests and maximizes space.

slides.title: Battle Against Aphids
slides.storyContext: Spring, and aphids swarm the young wheat. Grandpa spots them early. He walks to the field edge where marigolds bloom—they've attracted ladybugs. 'See? Ladybugs eat aphids. Nature's pest control. Free and harmless. No poison, no dead insects, just balance.'

example.problem: Grandpa notices aphids on wheat. Mix neem oil spray: 2% neem oil in water. Spray at sunrise. How often?
example.solution: Spray every 7-10 days during pest season. Repeat 3-4 times. Natural neem targets aphids without harming bees or soil microbes.

image.alt: Example 4: Neem Spray Application — Crop Production and Management

points.label: Hand Weeding
points.text: Pull weeds by hand (organic farms). Best after rain when soil is soft. Remove roots entirely to prevent regrowth.

points.label: Mulching
points.text: 2-3 inches of straw/leaves around plants prevents weed growth, retains moisture, regulates soil temperature.

points.label: Herbicide Risk
points.text: Chemical herbicides poison soil microbes and harm beneficial insects. Organic = manual + mulch + rotation.

points.label: Intercropping Example
points.text: Plant maize + beans together. Beans climb maize; maize shades soil. Both thrive; pests confused by mixed crop.

points.label: Companion Planting
points.text: Tomato + basil (pest control). Carrot + onion (pest control). Cucumber + marigold (attracts ladybugs).

points.label: Benefits
points.text: More yield per area, natural pest control, soil health, reduced pesticide need.

slides.title: Challenge 1: Design a Crop Rotation Plan

example.problem: Grandpa has 2 fields. Field A: wheat, Field B: needs a 3-year plan. What rotation works?
example.solution: Year 1: A-wheat, B-legume (chickpea). Year 2: A-legume, B-maize. Year 3: A-maize, B-wheat. Each field rests and gets legume nitrogen boost.

example.problem: Wheat field shows leaf-spot disease (fungal). Grandpa wants organic control. What three steps?
example.solution: 1) Remove & burn infected leaves (reduce disease source). 2) Spray sulfur powder or neem oil every 7 days. 3) Improve air circulation (thin weaker plants). Organic + targeted = saved crop.

example.problem: Rice crop (kharif) planted Jun 15. Monsoon rain is irregular. When to provide supplementary irrigation?
example.solution: Rice needs 5-7 cm water per week. Monitor: if 10 days pass without 5 cm rain, irrigate. Especially critical during grain-fill (Aug-Sep) when yield sets.

points.label: Clay Soil
points.text: Heavy, retains water (good), drains poorly (bad). Needs compost to improve drainage. Punjab's black soil is clay-rich.

points.label: Sandy Soil
points.text: Light, drains fast (good for waterlogging areas), doesn't retain nutrients (bad). Needs organic matter and frequent watering.

points.label: Loamy Soil
points.text: Best balance: clay + sand + silt. Retains moisture, drains well, holds nutrients. Ideal for most crops.

example.problem: Grandpa's field has heavy clay soil. How to improve it for better drainage and crop growth?
example.solution: Add 5-10 cm compost or sand + organic manure. Till to mix. Add straw mulch. In 2-3 seasons, soil becomes more loamy (better structure). Crop yields improve.

points.label: Quality Seeds
points.text: Use certified seeds: high purity, viability ≥80%, low moisture (8-12%). Store in cool, dry place.

points.label: Germination
points.text: Seeds need moisture, warmth, air. Dormant seeds wait for right conditions. Poor storage kills seeds.

points.label: Seed Rate
points.text: Amount of seed per unit area. Wheat: 125 kg/hectare. Too much = overcrowding; too little = sparse crop.

example.problem: Grandpa stores wheat seeds from this year's harvest for next season. Moisture: 12%. Where and how to store?
example.solution: Cool, dry, dark place (below 20°C, <60% humidity). Containers: jute bags or sealed drums. Check monthly for pests. Keep away from ammonia/fertilizer.

points.label: Prevention First
points.text: Rotation, clean seeds, resistant varieties, sanitation—prevent before treating.

points.label: Early Detection
points.text: Monitor crops weekly. Spot yellowing, spots, wilting, holes early. Act before spread.

points.label: Organic Arsenal
points.text: Neem, sulfur, Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis), ladybugs, yellow/blue traps, hand-pick large pests.

slides.title: Harvest Time & Lessons Learned
slides.storyContext: Harvest comes. Grandpa's wheat is golden, thick, disease-free. Priya helps gather the yield. 'Your rotation, compost, neem spray—they all worked!' Baldev nods: 'Yes. This is sustainable farming—we take from earth, we return to it. The soil stays alive for grandchildren.'

slides.title: Sustainable Farming

points.text: Crop rotation, composting, and natural pest control sustain soil health.
NPK nutrients, water timing, and seasonal crops must match.
Rabi (wheat, Oct-Mar), Kharif (rice, Jun-Sep), Zaid (summer vegetables).
Organic methods (neem, ladybugs, mulch) beat chemical pesticides—no poison, no dead soil.

slides.inSimpleWords: Respect soil, rotate crops, use nature wisely.

image.alt: Sustainable Farming — Crop Production and Management

subject: Science
title: Arjun's Lab Discoveries
hook: Arjun swabs different surfaces in his Delhi school: bathroom, kitchen, hands before/after washing. Under the microscope, he sees millions of bacteria. Some are helpful (yogurt bacteria). Some cause disease. How do we tell good from bad?

slides.title: Arjun's Microbe Quest
slides.inSimpleWords: Discover the invisible world of bacteria, viruses, and fungi.

slides.title: Swab Under the Microscope
slides.storyContext: Arjun grows bacteria cultures in petri dishes from different school locations. 'Mrs. Sharma, the bathroom sample has way more colonies than the kitchen!' She nods: 'Bacteria are everywhere—most harmless, some useful, few dangerous. Let's identify them.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria are tiny single-celled organisms everywhere.

image.alt: Swab Under the Microscope — Microorganisms - Friend and Foe

slides.title: What Are Bacteria?

points.label: Basic Structure
points.text: Single-celled organisms with no nucleus. Billions fit on a pinhead. Found in every habitat: soil, water, air, even inside us.

points.label: How They Reproduce
points.text: Binary fission: one cell splits into two identical cells. Under ideal conditions, bacteria double every 20 minutes.

points.label: Bacteria vs. Higher Cells
points.text: Prokaryotes (bacteria, no nucleus) vs. Eukaryotes (plant/animal cells, nucleus present). Bacteria evolved 3.5 billion years ago.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria are tiny cells without a nucleus that split to multiply.

slides.title: Example 1: Yogurt Bacteria

example.problem: Yogurt is made from Lactobacillus bacteria. How is this beneficial?
example.solution: Lactobacillus ferments milk sugar (lactose) into lactic acid, curdling milk into yogurt. This bacteria also aids human digestion and boosts immunity. A friendly helper microbe.

slides.inSimpleWords: Yogurt bacteria are helpful friends.

slides.title: Kitchen vs. Bathroom Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun's bathroom swab shows 800 bacterial colonies on the petri dish. Kitchen: only 200. Bathroom has more moisture, warm air, and organic matter—perfect for bacteria. Mrs. Sharma explains: 'More nutrients and humidity = faster growth.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Warm, moist places with food grow more bacteria.

points.text: Optimal bacterial growth: 37°C body temperature, moist environment, available food.

slides.title: Types of Microorganisms

points.label: Bacteria
points.text: Single-celled, no nucleus. Some helpful (gut bacteria aid digestion), some harmful (cause infections). Reproduce by splitting in two.

points.label: Fungi
points.text: Molds, yeasts, mushrooms. Fungi break down dead matter. Some edible (mushrooms), some toxic (food mold).

points.label: Viruses
points.text: Smaller than bacteria, need host cell to replicate. Cause colds, flu, COVID. Not living, but parasitic.

points.label: Protozoa
points.text: Single-celled protists. Some harmful (malaria parasite), some eat bacteria (benefit ecosystems).

slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria, fungi, and viruses are microorganisms.

image.alt: Types of Microorganisms — Microorganisms - Friend and Foe

slides.title: Bacterial Cell Structure

points.label: Cell Wall
points.text: Rigid outer layer protecting bacteria. Made of peptidoglycan. Gives shape: rod, sphere, or spiral.

points.label: Cytoplasm
points.text: Gel-like substance inside containing ribosomes (make proteins) and DNA (genetic blueprint).

points.label: Flagella (Tail)
points.text: Some bacteria have whip-like tails to move. Helps them find food and escape danger.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria have a cell wall, cytoplasm, and sometimes tails to move.

slides.title: Challenge 1: Design a Petri Dish Experiment
slides.storyContext: You want to test which household surfaces (phone, desk, doorknob) have the most bacteria. Design your swab experiment: What surface will you test? How will you keep samples uncontaminated? What will you compare?
slides.inSimpleWords: Plan an experiment to find bacteria around your home.

points.label: Tip
points.text: Sterile swabs, labelled petri dishes, incubate at 37°C for 24 hours, count colonies.

slides.title: Helpful vs. Harmful Microbes

points.label: Helpful Bacteria
points.text: Yogurt (Lactobacillus), gut bacteria (aid digestion), soil bacteria (fix nitrogen for plants), decomposers (break down waste).

points.label: Harmful Bacteria
points.text: Streptococcus (sore throat), E. coli (food poisoning), Salmonella (diarrhea), Tuberculosis (TB).

points.label: Prevention
points.text: Wash hands, clean food, cook properly, get vaccines, boil water, cover mouth when coughing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good microbes help us; bad ones need prevention.

image.alt: Helpful vs. Harmful Microbes — Microorganisms - Friend and Foe

slides.title: Example 2: Hand Washing Impact

example.problem: Arjun swabs his hands before and after washing. Before: 500 bacterial colonies. After washing with soap: 50 colonies. Why?
example.solution: Soap breaks bacterial cell membranes. Mechanical scrubbing removes bacteria. Hand washing reduces disease risk by ~50%. Essential hygiene habit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Washing removes 90% of harmful bacteria.

image.alt: Example 2: Hand Washing Impact — Microorganisms - Friend and Foe

slides.title: The Virus Discovery
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns viruses are even smaller—bacteria are giants compared to viruses. 'But Mrs. Sharma, how do we see viruses under a regular microscope?' 'We can't! They need electron microscopes. But we see their damage: cold sores, flu, chickenpox.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Viruses are smaller than bacteria and cause diseases.

points.text: Viruses only replicate inside host cells. Outside, they're dormant.

slides.title: How Viruses Attack

points.label: Infection Cycle
points.text: Virus enters host cell → hijacks cell machinery → makes copies → cell bursts → spreads to neighbors.

points.label: Common Viruses
points.text: Rhinovirus (cold), Influenza (flu), Coronavirus (COVID), Measles, Mumps.

points.label: Viral vs. Bacterial
points.text: Antibiotics kill bacteria (disrupt cell wall). Antivirals/vaccines work for viruses. Most viruses have no cure—prevention vital.

slides.inSimpleWords: Viruses hijack cells to copy themselves; vaccines prevent infection.

slides.title: Example 3: Cold Transmission

example.problem: Arjun sneezes in class. Rhinovirus travels 6 feet in air droplets. His classmate breathes them in 2 seconds later. Who gets sick first, why?
example.solution: Virus lands on respiratory mucosa of classmate. Infects cells in throat and nose. Symptoms (cough, sniffles) appear 1-3 days later as cells burst and immune system responds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Virus droplets spread when coughing or sneezing.

slides.title: Challenge 2: Prevent Virus Spread
slides.storyContext: If viruses spread via cough droplets, how would Arjun protect his classmates and himself during cold/flu season?
slides.inSimpleWords: Design a personal hygiene plan to stop virus transmission.

points.label: Answer Ideas
points.text: Mask in crowded places, hand hygiene, cover coughs/sneezes with elbow, stay home when sick, vaccinate.

slides.title: Fungi: Nature's Decomposers

points.label: Fungal Structure
points.text: Made of hyphae (thread-like filaments). Absorb nutrients from dead organic matter. Reproduce via spores.

points.label: Helpful Fungi
points.text: Mushrooms (food, medicine), baker's yeast (bread), Penicillium (antibiotic), mycorrhizae (help plant roots absorb water).

points.label: Harmful Fungi
points.text: Mold on bread (toxins), athlete's foot (skin infection), ringworm (contagious). Thrives in warm, damp places.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fungi break down dead matter and some are useful for food and medicine.

slides.title: Example 4: Mold on Bread

example.problem: Leftover bread in kitchen grows green mold in 3 days. Why not in the fridge?
example.solution: Mold spores are everywhere. On warm bread: spores germinate → hyphae grow → visible mold. Cold fridge stops spore germination. Frozen bread: no growth at all (spores dormant).

slides.inSimpleWords: Mold grows on bread left at room temperature but not in fridge.

slides.title: Mrs. Sharma's Lab Lesson
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma brings in cultures of helpful and harmful bacteria. 'Arjun, smell this yogurt culture—pleasant, right? Now this one from a wound swab—foul. Same cell type, different purpose. Your body is a battlefield where good and bad microbes fight daily.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Inside your body, microbes fight to survive.

slides.title: Human Microbiome

points.label: Gut Flora
points.text: Trillions of bacteria live in your intestines. They break down food, make vitamins (B12, K), train immune system.

points.label: Skin Microbiome
points.text: Bacteria like Staphylococcus live on skin harmlessly—until they breach skin barrier. Then infection.

points.label: Oral Flora
points.text: Bacteria in mouth cause plaque and cavities if you skip brushing. Proper hygiene keeps bad bacteria in check.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your body hosts trillions of helpful bacteria inside.

slides.title: Example 5: Antibiotics Save Lives

example.problem: Arjun gets a bacterial infection (Streptococcus) from a cut. Doctor prescribes penicillin. Why does it work?
example.solution: Penicillin disrupts bacterial cell wall synthesis. Bacteria cannot repair walls → cells burst → infection clears. But overuse breeds antibiotic-resistant 'superbugs.' Use antibiotics only when prescribed.

slides.inSimpleWords: Antibiotics kill bacteria by breaking their cell walls.

slides.title: Challenge 3: Antibiotic Resistance
slides.storyContext: If you take antibiotics for a viral cold (they don't work on viruses), you're helping bacteria develop resistance. Why is this dangerous? How can you avoid it?
slides.inSimpleWords: Understand why misusing antibiotics is harmful.

points.label: Key Insight
points.text: Some bacteria survive antibiotics → breed → offspring resist drug → superbug emerges. Use antibiotics ONLY for bacterial infections, and finish full course.

slides.title: Vaccines: Training Your Immune System

points.label: How Vaccines Work
points.text: Contain weakened or dead virus/bacteria. Immune system learns to recognize it. When real virus arrives, immune system is ready.

points.label: Famous Vaccines
points.text: Polio (oral drops in India), MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), COVID-19, Tetanus, Hepatitis B.

points.label: Herd Immunity
points.text: If 90%+ of population is vaccinated, disease cannot spread. Protects vulnerable infants and immunocompromised people.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vaccines teach your immune system to fight diseases before you catch them.

slides.title: Example 6: Polio Eradication in India

example.problem: In 1995, India had 50,000 polio cases/year. By 2014: zero cases. How?
example.solution: Nationwide vaccination campaigns (oral polio vaccine, OPV). Every child under 5 vaccinated regularly. Herd immunity reached ~95%. Polio virus had nowhere to hide → eliminated.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mass vaccination eliminated a deadly disease.

slides.title: Challenge 4: Design a Lab Safety Protocol
slides.storyContext: Arjun must handle bacteria cultures without contaminating them. What precautions should he take in the lab?
slides.inSimpleWords: Protect yourself and your experiment from contamination.

points.label: Best Practices
points.text: Sterile gloves, wash hands, flame-sterilize loops, work in biosafety cabinet, autoclave waste.

slides.title: Fermentation & Food Production

points.label: Bacteria in Fermentation
points.text: Lactobacillus ferments vegetables (pickles), dairy (cheese, yogurt), grains (bread). Produces lactic acid (preserves, adds tang). Ancient technology still used.

points.label: Fungal Fermentation
points.text: Yeast (Saccharomyces) ferments sugar into alcohol (beer, wine). Mold (Aspergillus) ferments soybeans (soy sauce, miso). These foods are nutritious and stable.

points.label: Health Benefits
points.text: Fermented foods provide probiotics (beneficial bacteria). Probiotics support gut health, digestion, immunity. Eating yogurt or pickles daily is healthy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fermentation by microbes creates healthy, nutritious foods.

slides.title: Example 6: Cheese Making

example.problem: Cheese is made by adding bacteria and enzymes to milk, then aging in caves. How do microbes transform milk to cheese?
example.solution: Starter bacteria (Lactobacillus) ferment lactose → lactic acid → milk curdles. Rennet enzyme cuts curds. Molds (Penicillium) in aging caves add flavor and texture. Result: Gruyere, Blue, Cheddar—microbes make them.

slides.inSimpleWords: Microbes transform milk into dozens of cheese varieties.

slides.title: Challenge 4: Probiotic Foods
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to boost his gut health with fermented foods. List 5 probiotic foods he could eat daily. What microbes make each one?
slides.inSimpleWords: Discover how traditional fermented foods support health.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Yogurt (Lactobacillus), pickles (Lactobacillus), kimchi (Lactobacillus), miso (Aspergillus), tempeh (Rhizopus).

slides.title: Antibiotic Discovery Moment
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma tells Arjun: 'In 1928, Alexander Fleming left a bacteria culture unattended. Mold contaminated it—but killed the bacteria! He discovered penicillin by accident. Sometimes accidents teach us the most.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Mold naturally kills bacteria—we turned this into antibiotics.

points.text: Penicillium fungus produces a chemical toxic to bacteria but safe for humans.

slides.title: Microbe Summary

points.text: Bacteria, fungi, and viruses are everywhere—most harmless, some useful, few dangerous.
Helpful microbes: yogurt bacteria (digestion), gut flora (vitamin production), decomposers (ecosystem), mycorrhizae (plant symbiosis).
Fermented foods (yogurt, cheese, pickles) provide probiotics for health.
Harmful microbes need prevention: hygiene, vaccines, antibiotics, avoiding contamination.
Arjun's lab proves: understanding microbes keeps communities healthy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Not all microbes are bad—some are essential.

image.alt: Microbe Summary — Microorganisms - Friend and Foe

subject: Science
title: Priya's Diwali Diya Experiment
hook: During Diwali celebrations in Delhi, Priya lights dozens of oil diyas (earthen lamps). 'Why does the flame burn?' she wonders. Her science teacher explains: combustion needs three things—fuel, oxygen, and heat. Remove any one, the flame dies.

slides.title: Priya's Combustion Adventure
